11.1.b:
A painful replacement asks two questions in turn: is it loose, and is it infected?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "a painful loose hip — what do you think first?"
- "A loose implant is **septic until proved otherwise**."
- "So the **infection work-up** comes before any revision."
- "Septic and aseptic loosening are treated completely differently."

### Definition of Loosening
Before splitting septic from aseptic, we need a clear definition.
- **Loosening** is failed fixation: never achieved, or lost later
- It has **no active mechanical cause** behind it
- It is a **radiographic** diagnosis; the clinic only raises the suspicion (Handbook)

| Still loosening, after… | Not loosening — a cause is active |
|---|---|
| a **previous dislocation** | an **acute fracture** |
| a **healed fracture** | an **active dislocation** |

- Acute fracture → 15 Periprosthetic fractures · active dislocation → 13 Instability

### Septic versus Aseptic Loosening
Every loose implant then goes down one of two roads.
- The first split is **septic** versus **aseptic** loosening
- It comes first, because the treatment differs completely
- Septic → 12 Periprosthetic joint infection · aseptic → 14 Aseptic loosening

CLINICAL PEARL — beware septic loosening
- Exclude **septic loosening** even when the case looks aseptic (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Loose in the **first few years**? Think infection or failed fixation, not wear

MEMORY HOOK — guilty until proved innocent
- Every loose implant is an infection suspect until the cultures give it an alibi.

### Sources of Pain Without Loosening
Pain can also come from a fixed implant, or from outside the joint.

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Loose implant | septic or aseptic loosening |
| Fixed implant, hip | well-fixed cementless stem: **modulus mismatch** |
| Fixed implant, knee | tibial **overhang** irritating the medial ligament · **anterior knee pain**, patellar maltracking |
| Leg-length discrepancy | **abductor strain** and ache (Prof Khaled Fawzy) |
| Outside the hip | the **lumbar spine**, the **sacroiliac joint**, the knee |
| Outside the knee | the **hip** and the spine refer pain to the knee |

- LLD also lengthens the abductor work: higher joint force, later wear and loosening
- So the work-up runs: story, bloods, films, then other scans

11.2.b:
The story comes first, because it often points to infection, the cup or the stem.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does the pain point the way?"
- "**Start-up** and weight-bearing pain = aseptic; **night** pain = septic."
- "**Groin** pain points to the cup; **thigh** pain to the stem."
- "The primary goal is to **exclude septic loosening**."

### Timing of Pain
The rhythm of the pain separates the two roads.

| Pain | Aseptic loosening | Septic loosening |
|---|---|---|
| When | activity, **start-up** | **constant** |
| Worse | on **weight bearing** | at **night** |

- Aseptic pain comes with load, because the loose implant settles
- Most septic patients are **afebrile** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- So a normal temperature never rules infection out

MEMORY HOOK — morning and midnight
- Aseptic aches when it starts; septic aches in the dark.

### Site of Pain
The site of the pain names the suspect part.
- **Groin** pain points to the **cup**
- **Thigh** pain points to the **stem**
- Anterior pain is vaguer; the examination finds the true source

PITFALL — thigh pain is not always a loose stem
- A well-fixed cementless stem can hurt: a stiff tip in a flexible femur
- The spine and knee also mimic hip pain
- Say → "**examine the spine and knee, and check fixation, before blaming the stem**"

### Physical Examination
Then examine the whole patient, not just the scar.

#### Signs of Infection
- General: **fever**, anorexia, malaise (Handbook)
- Local: red, hot, tender, swollen; a collection or a **sinus**
- Ask about **previous discharge** or infection (Prof Mahmoud Abdel Karim)

#### Mechanical and Neurological Assessment
- Watch the **gait** and measure the **ROM** (range of motion)
- Test the abductors: **Trendelenburg** test
- Check **LLD** (leg-length discrepancy): true lengths, and blocks for apparent length
- A reduced **prior dislocation**, or obesity, points to a **mechanical** cause
- Check the neurology to exclude **nerve injury**

The story raises the suspicion; the laboratory confirms or excludes infection.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which tests exclude infection?"
- "**ESR** and **CRP**, with aspiration if needed, to **exclude infection**."
- "At revision, antibiotics wait for cultures: one dose before, one after."
- "Send tissue for Gram stain and culture; add **TB** in chronic referred cases."

### Preoperative Screening
Bloods are the screen for every painful replacement.
- **ESR** (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and **CRP** (C-reactive protein) come first
- Add a **CBC** (leukocytosis, left shift) and **blood cultures** (Handbook)
- Both markers normal: ≈5% are still infected, NPV (negative predictive value) **95%**
- **Aspirate** when infection is still possible
- Thresholds, aspiration technique and their traps → 12 Periprosthetic joint infection

### Intraoperative Cultures
Even a case that looks aseptic is cultured in theatre.

#### Antibiotic Timing
- **Antibiotics are withheld** until the cultures return (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- The exception: one dose before surgery and one after
[[FIG: Fig 11.1 · 11.3
- Course case: CRP 30, ESR 100; all implants out, cultures sent, antibiotics held

#### Specimens
- Tissue for **Gram stain**, **aerobic** and **anaerobic** culture
- Add **TB** culture in chronic, referred cases
[[FIG: Fig 11.2 · 11.3
- Then follow with **serial ESR and CRP**

MEMORY HOOK — fingerprints first
- Take the fingerprints (cultures) before you wipe the scene (antibiotics).

11.4.b:
With infection being excluded, the films ask the mechanical question: is it loose?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do films show loosening?"
- "**AP and lateral** films down to the stem tip, compared over time."
- "**Lucency** is the most important sign; **migration** the most reliable."
- "A **periosteal reaction** makes you think of infection."

### Standard Views
Two views are the minimum, and the whole stem must show.
- Take **AP and lateral** views down to the **stem tip**
- Accuracy is **90%** on the femoral side (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- But only **65%** on the acetabular side: cup loosening is often missed
- Compare with old films taken the same way (Campbell)
- **10°** of limb rotation can fake, or hide, stem migration

### Radiographic Signs of Loosening
Five signs say loose; two lines need a second look.

#### Principal Signs

| Sign (Handbook) | Weight |
|---|---|
| **Lucency** | the most important |
| **Migration** or change in position | the most reliable |
| **Implant failure**: broken screws, broken stem | a loose implant |
| **Cement-mantle fracture** | a loose implant |
| Motion on **stress or weight-bearing** views | loose, even when serial films look the same |

- Measure migration from a fixed point: **greater-trochanter tip**, or head–neck junction, to the **stem tip**

MEMORY HOOK — the line and the move
- A line can be argued about, but a moving implant cannot: migration is the most reliable sign.

#### Associated Findings
- A **thin sclerotic line** beside a stable lucency is a **fibrous border**
- A **periosteal reaction** points to **infection**
- Plain films rarely separate septic from aseptic loosening (Handbook)
- Septic picture: periostitis, reactive bone, **endosteal scalloping**, lucency growing **week by week** → 12

11.5.b:
Lucency is the commonest finding, so the real question is when a line means loose.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when does a lucent line mean loose?"
- "**Cement–metal** lucency always means loosening."
- "Elsewhere a line counts only if **2 mm or more** and **new or progressive**."
- "Cemented stem → **Harris**; cementless stem → **Engh**; cup → **3 zones**; knee → **Knee Society**."

### Interface Assessment
Where the line sits decides how much it matters.

#### Significance by Interface

| Interface | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cement–metal** | always loosening, whatever its width: nothing debonds normally |
| **Cement–bone**, or cementless | counts only if **2 mm or more** and **new or progressive** |

- A stable line is benign, or part of the design

MEMORY HOOK — no friendly divorce
- Cement and metal never separate on friendly terms: any gap between them means loosening.

#### Lines Not Indicating Loosening
- A line seen on the first post-op film may be implant on cancellous bone (Handbook)
- Lines in **50–100%** of the interface, unchanged at **5 years**, mean **poor cementing**
- A polished taper-slip stem (**Exeter**) shows a small early shoulder gap: expected, not loosening
- Gruen and DeLee–Charnley zones → 06 Post-op radiograph

### Harris Criteria
Harris grades a cemented stem from possible to definite.

#### Grades

| Grade | Sign (Campbell; Prof Sherif Khaled) |
|---|---|
| **Possible** | incomplete lucency, **>50%** of the cement interface |
| **Probable** | **complete** lucency around the cement |
| **Definite** | stem or cement fracture · stem–cement lucency · change in stem position |

#### Radiographic Examples
- Incomplete lines show as gaps along part of the mantle
[[FIG: Fig 11.3 · 11.5
- Complete lines surround the whole stem
[[FIG: Fig 11.4 · 11.5
- Case: **lateral mantle fracture**, lines almost all round, so definitely loose
[[FIG: Fig 11.5 · 11.5
- He had no symptoms, so he was followed

### Engh Classification
Engh grades a cementless stem by how the bone holds it.

#### Grades

| Grade | Signs (Prof Sherif Khaled; Campbell) |
|---|---|
| **Stable bony ingrowth**: fixed | **spot welds**, reactive bone lines · calcar atrophy, no pedestal |
| **Stable fibrous**: stable | no spot welds, no migration · **parallel sclerotic lines** about **1 mm** from the stem |
| **Unstable fibrous**: loose | **progressive** lines, wider at the ends · subsidence, varus drift · **pedestal** at the tip |

- Stable fibrous fixation shows neither loosening nor ingrowth on the film

#### Radiographic Features
- **Spot welds**: endosteal bone bridging to the coating
[[FIG: Fig 11.6 · 11.5
- They sit near the end of an extensive coating
- Calcar atrophy here is **stress shielding**, not loosening
- A diaphyseal fit unloads the proximal femur, which remodels
- Unstable: progressive lines and **subsidence**
[[FIG: Fig 11.7 · 11.5
- A **pedestal** is bone that stops the stem tip
[[FIG: Fig 11.8 · 11.5

PITFALL — thin proximal bone is not a loose stem
- Thin proximal bone with distal spot welds is **load bypass**
- Say → "**spot welds mean the stem is well fixed, even with thin proximal bone**"

[[FIG: Fig 11.9 · 11.5

PITFALL — no pedestal under cement
- A **pedestal** is a cementless sign only (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Under a cemented stem, the distal opacity is the **cement plug**

### Acetabular Component
The cup is read by migration and by lines in its three zones.
- Zones (DeLee–Charnley): **1** superior, **2** middle, **3** inferior third
- An **inclination change** alone means a loose cup, cemented or cementless (Campbell)

#### Cementless Cup
- **Migration** of more than **2–5 mm** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Lines in **3 zones**, over **2 mm**, progressive over **2 years**
- Also loose: a broken screw, medialisation, protrusio or **upward migration**
[[FIG: Fig 11.10 · 11.5
- Gross migration and tilt leave no doubt
[[FIG: Fig 11.11 · 11.5
- Engh: stable · probably unstable (progressive lines) · definitely unstable (measurable migration)

#### Cemented Cup
- Lucency **all round**, over **2 mm** and progressive, in **3 zones**
- **Superior or medial migration**, and wear
[[FIG: Fig 11.12 · 11.5
- Medial migration ends in **protrusio**, with or without a medial-wall fracture
- Cup or cement fracture is rare
- Hodgkinson: lines in 3 zones, **94%** loose at revision · 2 zones **71%** · 1 zone **7%**
- So the extent of the line matters more than its width

### Knee Society Radiographic Evaluation
The knee has its own zone score (1989), read on AP and lateral films.
- Zones: **7** tibial on the AP, **3** tibial and **7** femoral on the lateral, **5** patellar
[[FIG: Fig 11.13 · 11.5
- Each zone is scored by the width and extent of its lucency

| Tibial score | Meaning (Prof Sherif Khaled; Campbell) |
|---|---|
| **≤4**, non-progressive | probably insignificant |
| **5–9** | close follow-up for progression |
| **≥10** | possible or impending failure, whatever the symptoms |

- Knee alignment angles on the same form → 10 TKA radiographs

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Cement–metal always · elsewhere 2 mm and growing · Harris cemented · Engh cementless · 3 zones cup · Knee Society knee**

11.6.b:
When plain films cannot see behind the metal, other images step in.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when do you go beyond plain films?"
- "**Arthrography** or **CT** shows lucencies hidden behind metal."
- "A loose cementless cup with a **cavitary defect** needs **CT** for the medial wall."
- "Nuclear scans belong to the infection work-up."

### Arthrography and CT
A dense implant can hide the very line we look for.
- **Arthrography** or **CT** shows lucencies hidden behind metal

### CT for Cavitary Defects
A loose cup can leave a hole behind it.
- A loose cementless cup with a **cavitary defect** gets a **CT**
[[FIG: Fig 11.14 · 11.6
- The CT shows the **medial wall** before revision
[[FIG: Fig 11.15 · 11.6
- Classifying and filling the defect → 14 Aseptic loosening & bone defects

Scans answer the septic question, not the loose one.
- **Technetium** is hot in both; **indium** is hot only when septic (Handbook)
- A bone scan stays positive for **1–2 years** after surgery
- Details → 12 Periprosthetic joint infection
